label: Chapter 14
title: Demas and the Pillar of Salt

blocks.p: Then Christian and Hopeful drew ahead of them again, and went on until they came to a pleasant plain called Ease, where they walked with great contentment. But the plain was narrow, so they were soon across it. At the far side of the plain was a little hill called Lucre, and in that hill a silver mine. Some who had come that way before had turned aside to see it, because it was such a rare thing; but going too near the edge of the pit, the ground gave way under them, and they were killed. Others had been maimed there, and to their dying day were never themselves again.

Then I saw in my dream that a little off the road, across from the silver mine, stood Demas, like a gentleman, calling out to travelers to come and see. He said to Christian and his companion, “Hello there! Turn aside this way, and I’ll show you something.”
“What could be worth turning us out of the way to see it?” said Christian.
“Here is a silver mine, and some people digging in it for treasure. If you come, with a little effort you can make yourselves rich.”
“Let’s go and see,” said Hopeful.

“Not I,” said Christian. “I’ve heard of this place before, and how many have been killed here. Besides, treasure is a snare to those who seek it, because it holds them back on their pilgrimage.” Then Christian called to Demas, “Isn’t the place dangerous? Hasn’t it held back many on their pilgrimage?” [Hos. 14:8]
“Not very dangerous,” said Demas, “except to the careless.” But he blushed as he said it.
“Let’s not take a single step toward it,” said Christian to Hopeful, “but keep on our way.”
“I’ll guarantee you,” said Hopeful, “when Self-Interest comes up, if he gets the same invitation we did, he’ll turn in there to see.”
“No doubt of it, for his principles lead him that way; and it’s a hundred to one he dies there.”
Then Demas called again: “But won’t you come over and see?”

Christian answered him bluntly. “Demas, you are an enemy to the right ways of the Lord of this road, and you have already been condemned by one of His Majesty’s judges for your own turning aside. [2 Tim. 4:10] Why are you trying to bring us under the same condemnation? Besides, if we turn aside at all, our Lord and King will certainly hear of it, and will put us to shame on the very day we would want to stand before him with confidence.”
Demas called out again that he was one of their brotherhood too, and that if they would wait a little, he would walk with them himself.
“What is your name?” said Christian. “Isn’t it the one I just called you?”
“Yes, my name is Demas. I am a son of Abraham.”

“I know you,” said Christian. “Gehazi was your great-grandfather, and Judas your father, and you have walked in their steps. [2 Kings 5:20; Matt. 26:14-15; 27:1-5] This is nothing but a devilish trick of yours. Your father was hanged as a traitor, and you deserve no better. You can be sure that when we come to the King, we will tell him how you behaved.”
And so they went on their way.

By this time Self-Interest and his companions had come back into sight, and at the very first wave of the hand they went over to Demas. Whether they fell into the pit looking over its edge, or went down to dig, or were smothered at the bottom by the poisonous air that commonly rises there, I am not certain. But this I observed: they were never seen on the road again. Then Christian sang:

v: Self-Interest and silver Demas both agree:
one calls, the other runs, so he can be
a sharer in his treasure; men like these
stop in this world, and go no further than they please.

blocks.p: Now I saw that just on the other side of this plain, the pilgrims came to a place where an old monument stood close beside the highway. At the sight of it they were both troubled, because of its strange shape; for it looked to them as if it had been a woman turned into the shape of a pillar. They stood there looking and looking at it, but for a while could make nothing of it. At last Hopeful spotted some writing above its head, in an unusual script. He was no scholar, so he called to Christian, who was learned, to see if he could work out what it said. Christian came, and after a little piecing of the letters together, he found it said this: Remember Lot’s wife. He read it to his companion, and they both concluded that this was the pillar of salt that Lot’s wife was turned into for looking back with a covetous heart as she was fleeing Sodom for safety. [Gen. 19:26] This sudden and astonishing sight started the following conversation.

“Ah, my brother,” said Christian, “this sight has come at just the right time, right after Demas invited us over to look at the Hill Lucre. If we had gone over as he wanted, and as you were inclined to do, my brother, we might, for all I know, have been made like this woman: a spectacle for those who come after us.”

“I’m sorry I was so foolish,” said Hopeful, “and I wonder that I am not standing here like Lot’s wife. For what was the difference between her sin and mine? She only looked back; I had a desire to go and see. Let grace be praised, and let me be ashamed that such a thing was ever in my heart.”

“Let’s take note of what we see here, to help us in time to come. This woman escaped one judgment, because she did not die in the destruction of Sodom; yet she was destroyed by another, for here she stands, turned into a pillar of salt.”

“True. And she can be both a warning and an example to us: a warning to shun her sin, and a sign of the judgment that will overtake anyone this warning does not stop. In the same way Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, with the two hundred and fifty men who perished in their sin, became a sign and example for others to beware. [Num. 26:9-10] But above everything, one thing amazes me. How can Demas and his friends stand there so confidently looking for that treasure, when this woman, just for looking back at it (for we don’t read that she stepped one foot out of the way), was turned into a pillar of salt? And especially since the judgment that overtook her made her an example within sight of where they are. They can’t help seeing her, if they would only lift up their eyes.”

“It is a thing to wonder at,” said Christian, “and it shows that their hearts have grown desperate. I can’t think of anyone to compare them to so well as people who pick pockets in front of the judge, or cut purses under the gallows. It is said of the men of Sodom that they were exceedingly wicked, because they sinned before the Lord, that is, right in his sight, and in spite of all the kindness he had shown them [Gen. 13:13]; for the land of Sodom was like the garden of Eden in those days. [Gen. 13:10] This provoked him all the more, and made their punishment as hot as the fire of the Lord out of heaven could make it. And it is only reasonable to conclude that people like these, who sin in plain sight, and in spite of the examples set continually before them to warn them, must share in the severest judgments.”

“No doubt you have spoken the truth,” said Hopeful. “But what a mercy it is that neither you nor, especially, I have been made into such an example! This gives us reason to thank God, to fear him, and always to remember Lot’s wife.”

I saw then that they went on their way to a pleasant river, which David the king called “the river of God,” but John “the river of the water of life.” [Ps. 65:9; Rev. 22; Ezek. 47] Their road ran right along the bank of the river, and here Christian and his companion walked with great delight. They drank the water of the river too, which was pleasant and refreshing to their weary spirits. Besides this, on both banks of the river grew green trees bearing every kind of fruit, and the leaves of the trees were good for medicine. They delighted in the fruit of these trees, and they ate the leaves to ward off overeating and the other illnesses that come to those who overheat their blood with travel. On both sides of the river there was also a meadow, beautifully adorned with lilies and green all year round. In this meadow they lay down and slept, for here they could lie down in safety. When they woke, they gathered fruit from the trees again, and drank again from the river, and then lay down again to sleep. [Ps. 23:2; Isa. 14:30] They did this for several days and nights. Then they sang:

v: See how these crystal streams so gently glide
to comfort pilgrims by the highway side;
the meadows green, besides their fragrant smell,
yield them good things to eat; and he who can tell
what pleasant fruit, and leaves, these trees supply,
will soon sell all he has, this field to buy.

blocks.p: So when they were ready to go on (for they were not yet at their journey’s end), they ate and drank, and set out.
